title: Distance from an activation to the J-space
takeaway: The equation defines how far an activation sits from the J-space: the smallest reconstruction error over every choice of $k$ J-lens vectors. The projection that achieves that minimum is the activation's J-space component, and what is left over is the residual the paper's ablation interventions keep.
walkthrough:
This equation gives a distance from a point in activation space to the J-space, and in doing so pins down two quantities the rest of the paper uses informally: the J-space component of an activation and its residual. It sits in the appendix that puts the [[j-space-formalization]] on a formal footing.

The objects come first. $v_1, \dots, v_n$ are the [[j-lens-vector]]s at one layer, one direction in [[residual-stream]] space for each token of the [[tokenizer-vocabulary]]. $x$ is an activation at that layer. $S$ is a subset of the vocabulary indices, and $|S| = k$ fixes its size at the allowable sparsity level. $k$ is a free parameter; the paper typically sets it near 25, the number of lens vectors it measures as meaningfully active at one time.

$\operatorname{span}\{v_i : i \in S\}$ is written as a span, but the surrounding text restricts it to nonnegative combinations of that particular choice of $k$ vectors, which makes it a $k$-dimensional cone. $\mathcal{F}$ is the union of these cones over every size-$k$ subset ([[union-of-cones]]), and that union is the [[j-space]]. It is not a subspace, because which $k$ vectors get used is part of the answer.

The second line is a search. For a given subset $S$, $\Pi_S$ projects $x$ orthogonally onto the span of those $k$ vectors, and $\| x - \Pi_S x \|$ measures how much of $x$ the projection fails to capture. The minimum of that error over all size-$k$ subsets is $d_\mathcal{F}(x)$, the Euclidean distance from $x$ to the nearest cone. The equality on the right states the same quantity directly, as the distance to the closest point $y$ anywhere in $\mathcal{F}$.

Two pieces fall out of whichever subset wins. $\Pi_S x$ is the [[j-space-component]] of $x$, the part of the activation the workspace vectors can account for. The leftover $x - \Pi_S x$ is the residual, and it is what the activation is reduced to when [[j-space-ablation]] strips the workspace contents out.

Searching every size-$k$ subset is not tractable, so the minimizing set is found in practice by [[gradient-pursuit]], a greedy algorithm that adds one vector at a time ([[sparse-decomposition]]).

A small $d_\mathcal{F}(x)$ would mean the activation lies nearly inside the workspace. The measurement runs the other way for most activations: the top-$K$ lens vectors explain under 10% of activation variance beyond a same-size random control ([[excess-variance-explained]]), so the distance stays large and the J-space accounts for a thin slice of what the model is holding.

terms.definition: The distance function from an activation $x$ to the J-space: the smallest Euclidean error left after projecting $x$ onto the span of any $k$ J-lens vectors. Small values mean the activation is close to being a sparse nonnegative sum of lens vectors.
The J-space itself, written as a set: the union, over every size-$k$ subset of the vocabulary, of the cone of nonnegative combinations of those $k$ J-lens vectors.
An activation at one layer, that is, a residual-stream vector at one token position. It is the point whose distance to the J-space is being measured.
The J-lens vectors at that layer, one per vocabulary token. Each is the direction that, on average across contexts, disposes the model to say that token later.
The number of vocabulary vectors, equal to the tokenizer's vocabulary size $n_{\text{vocab}}$. It exceeds the residual-stream width, which is what makes the set overcomplete.
The allowable sparsity level: how many J-lens vectors may carry nonzero coefficients. Without fixing $k$ the definition is empty, because the full set of lens vectors spans the whole residual stream.
A subset of the vocabulary indices, constrained to hold exactly $k$ of them. The minimization ranges over every such subset.
The set of combinations of the $k$ chosen lens vectors. The paper restricts the coefficients to be nonnegative, so this is a polyhedral cone rather than a linear subspace.
Orthogonal projection onto the span of the $k$ vectors indexed by $S$: the linear map sending $x$ to the closest point in that span.
The J-space component of $x$: the part of the activation that the winning set of $k$ lens vectors can reconstruct. This is what the paper means when it says a concept is 'in' the workspace.

The residual, or non-J-space component: everything in the activation the workspace vectors do not account for. It is the term the paper's ablation interventions leave behind after removing the J-space part.
The Euclidean norm on residual-stream vectors. The paper uses both notations for the same quantity in the two halves of the equation.
A point of $\mathcal{F}$, used in the right-hand form of the definition; the minimum over all such $y$ is the same distance as the minimum over subsets.
The minimization over all size-$k$ subsets of the vocabulary. It is combinatorial and is not computed exhaustively; gradient pursuit approximates the winning subset.
The greedy sparse-approximation algorithm the paper uses to find a nonnegative combination of $k$ lens vectors that reconstructs an activation well, standing in for the exact minimization.
The set of activation-space points expressible as a sparse nonnegative combination of J-lens vectors; the candidate global workspace this equation measures distance to.

numbers.meaning: The sparsity level, the one free parameter in the definition. The paper calls the choice somewhat arbitrary and varies it across experiments, since nothing in the model fixes a single correct value.

The value $k$ typically takes, written as $k \approx 25$. It comes from the occupancy measurement: across the workspace layers, the number of lens vectors that beat a random control in reconstructing an activation plateaus around 25 in the median case.
The dimension of each cone, one per size-$k$ subset. The J-space is a union of these cones, so it has no single dimension of its own even though every piece of it has dimension $k$.

The ceiling on the fraction of activation variance the J-space component carries, measured as variance explained by the top-$K$ lens vectors in excess of a same-size random control, with $K$ set to the median occupancy at each workspace layer. It varies by layer but never exceeds 10%, which is the paper's evidence that activations are dominated by information outside the workspace.

The overcompleteness condition: more lens vectors than residual-stream dimensions. It is why the vectors typically span the whole space, why no decomposition is unique, and therefore why the sparsity constraint $|S| = k$ is needed for the distance to be nonzero.
The subsets are of exact size $k$. Because the cones for smaller subsets are faces of the size-$k$ cones, allowing fewer vectors would not change the minimum.
